A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same user study and proxy-LLM evaluation. All 19 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Figures, tables, and study content can be matched across the substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original results from 94 participants providing 470 evaluations of 90 PrivacyLens scenarios, alongside repeated evaluations from five proxy LLMs and qualitative analysis.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds pooled-judge comparisons, coded-theme frequencies, and quantitative explanation-similarity results.

M1.justification: Both versions use GPT-5 with the PrivacyLens privacy-enhancing prompt to generate responses and the same five proxy LLMs to judge them. v2 discloses prompt templates and adds evaluation analyses without establishing a change to the underlying generation or judging procedure.

E1.justification: Both use the same 90 PrivacyLens scenarios and 94 U.S.-based, English-fluent adult participants. The tasks and population remain unchanged. Newly discussed examples and analyses use the existing study material.

E2.justification: The five individual proxy models are unchanged. However, v2 adds an 'All Proxy LLMs' pooled comparator to the rating-range comparison and Spearman correlation table (Figure 2 and Table 3). v1 already pooled models for agreement analysis, but not in these corresponding comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Universal Sentence Encoder similarity for comparing explanations, pooled range/correlation analyses over 25 proxy judgments, and inspection of the 10 most aligned and 10 most divergent scenarios. v1's qualitative comparison focused on disagreement cases. The original survey settings, model configurations, and generation defaults are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the analysis through coded explanation frequencies, quantitative semantic similarity, and tests of whether pooling judges captures human variability. It also examines aligned cases and introduces examples 47 and 32, while removing extended case discussions such as scenarios 20, 50, 60, and 11. These changes materially revise the analytical support for the findings.

E5.justification: Both results sections use five runs per proxy model, report within-scenario dispersion, and use the same Spearman significance notation at p < 0.001. v2 adds results under these practices without introducing new seeds, confidence intervals, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. v1's isolated 'five or more' wording does not establish a different run count.

E6.justification: The original agreement scores, individual-model correlations, rating distributions, and demographics are retained. v2 substantially expands the results with pooled correlations of 0.33 for helpfulness and 0.59 for privacy (Table 3), explanation similarities of 0.18–0.27 for participants versus 0.66–0.85 for individual proxy LLMs (Table 4), and coded-theme frequencies (Section 4.1). The unchanged individual correlations include Mistral's 0.07 privacy correlation.

T1.justification: The conceptual Contextual Integrity framework remains unchanged. Neither version supplies mathematical theorems or proofs, and the added semantic-similarity measurement introduces no new formal definition or derivation.

C1.justification: Both versions retain RQ1–RQ3 and the central claims: users differ in their evaluations, proxy judges are more consistent but inadequately capture human judgments and diversity, and human involvement and personalization deserve attention. The revised title and additional evidence do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies generalization limits from using one response generator, five proxy models with particular prompting setups, and U.S.-based English-fluent participants. It also interprets the new pooled ratings and coded explanations. The central explanation based on individual preferences and contextual nuances remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds generation and judging prompt templates (A.2–A.3), A100 evaluation times (Table 2), recruitment-balancing explanations, and identifier-removal details. A.4 promises a future data/code release without supplying released artifacts. These disclosures improve documentation, although v1 Figure 1's verbatim survey questions are condensed into labels in v2.

R1.justification: v2 adds directly relevant human–LLM judging research, including Meisenbacher et al., Pan et al., and Juneja et al., and positions its findings alongside that work in Section 5. It also connects the proposed evaluation taxonomy to prior disagreement and subjective-annotation research. The principal Contextual Integrity and PrivacyLens framing remains.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites and condenses existing prose, retitles the paper to emphasize proxy judges, reorganizes methods and results, merges conclusion and discussion, and moves ethical considerations. Its appendix becomes a structured set of subsections. This constitutes substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column ACM manuscript to two columns. Figure 1 is redrawn; v1 Figure 4 is split across v2 Figures 2 and 6 with an added pooled panel. Several original plots and the correlation table move to the appendix, while runtime and semantic-similarity tables are added. The example screenshot is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 provides a limited net improvement: pooled-judge and explanation analyses strengthen support for the existing findings, while prompt templates and explicit limitations improve transparency. These gains are tempered by the loss of several detailed case discussions and verbatim survey-question wording. The artifact release remains a future plan, so reproducibility is only partially improved.
